cells.tense: You are at the point where what you kept and what you let go of sit evenly.
cells.act: weigh what it costs them against what it gives
cells.ask: Next time someone close brings you a feeling, say what it costs them and what it gives them, out loud, and stop there. Nothing after it.
cells.core:
You can hold two weights at once: what a feeling costs someone and what it gives them, and say both plainly without making a tally. At the table with the people close to you, that's what lets a hard thing be spoken and then set down. What you release, you release because it's finished, and the next thing gets ground to grow in.

That evenness costs something. It asks you to name the cost before anyone asks you to, and to stay there while it's taken in. So it isn't yours to carry by yourself. Say the cost out loud, say what it gives, and hold your ground while the answer comes. You'll hear the difference between weighing a feeling and being fair about it. The balance holds.
cells.sheetLine: You let go of what's finished and keep what grows.
cells.verb: composting what's finished so what's still growing has ground
cells.place: the table where you take in what the people close to you are feeling

cells.tense: You will keep wrapping up what matters to them before anyone there has had it long enough.
cells.act: ask how it feels to them and stay with the answer
cells.ask: Pick one shared thing you'd rather finish. Ask the person in it how it lands for them, and sit for a minute with whatever comes back, without fixing it.
cells.core:
A thing ends here because it's actually done, and the people near you can feel the ending came from something real. What's happening instead is that endings get decided long before the room arrives. You can see what a thing will become, and from that far point you tidy it away early. The people in it are still inside it.

Before you close the next one, ask the person who's still in it how it lands for them. Sit with their answer a minute without explaining what you already saw. That isn't agreeing to keep it. It's finding out what the thing holds for them before you decide its worth. Once you've heard it, the endings you make will be the ones that are actually finished.

cells.verb: composting what's finished so what's still growing has ground

cells.tense: You had a way of feeling alongside people, and you've stood back from it.
cells.act: feed the drive a little at a time
cells.ask: Take up something you enjoy, small and yours, and give it your full attention while you're in it.
cells.core:
You used to feel alongside people, and somewhere along the way you stopped arriving. You still turn up. The connection is happening around you rather than in you, and it's gone on long enough that it reads as your nature. It isn't. When the fire is low, the part of you that takes in what others feel runs on what the fire gives it, and when the fuel runs out you go quiet.

Don't try to force the feeling back. Feed the fire instead. Take up something you enjoy, small and yours, with no one you're doing it for, and give it your full attention while you're in it. Then go back to it a few days later. Wanting comes first, and the feeling alongside comes back once you're standing in your own warmth again.
cells.sheetLine: You've stood back so long it looks like who you are.
cells.verb: composting what's finished so what's still growing has ground
cells.place: the table where you take in what the people close to you are feeling

cells.tense: You've been ending what's finished for the people around you and calling it nothing.
cells.act: cut through the inertia with one decisive act
cells.ask: Find the thing you've been letting run on out of politeness, and end it in one sentence, owing no explanation to anyone.
cells.core:
The people close to you are lighter because of something you do — you let a shared thing finish when it's finished, and make ground for something else to start. Your version is that you just got on with it. The ending was yours, and it's been kept off the record so long that you can't see it as a thing you do.

An earlier form of it was yours before the careful version: the clean cut, the decision made and stood by, nothing owed. Try that on the thing you've been letting run on out of politeness. End it — one sentence, nothing to argue. You'll feel the cut land the way it used to, and the shape of the situation will come clear.
cells.sheetLine: You've been ending what's done and calling it nothing.
cells.verb: composting what's finished so what's still growing has ground
cells.place: the table where you take in what the people close to you are feeling
